newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ATHLETICS-MONEY SPARKS DRUG USE AMONG ROMANIAN ATHLETES.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-MONEY SPARKS DRUG USE AMONG ROMANIAN ATHLETES.

text.p: Poverty at home and the lure of handsome rewards abroad have sparked an unprecedented string of track and field doping scandals in Romania since the fall of communism eight years ago.
"Money pushes Romanian athletes to put their sports careers at risk," Romanian athletic federation president Iolanda Balas said in an interview.
With the national wage in Romania averaging around $60 a month, the money now available for successful athletes has never looked more attractive.

Ion Puica, who coached his wife Maricica to the 3,000 metres title at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, said freedom of movement in the post-communist era allowed athletes now to enter well-paid international events.
"The situation is unprecedented in Romanian sports," Puica said. "Before 1989, we were faced with only one or two doping cases throughout the four-year gap between Olympics.
"It's easy now for a Romanian athlete to find stanozolol, for instance, and to take it."
Puica, 67, was appointed sports advisor to Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea this year.
The latest drugs case involves the country's best women's long-distance runner, Iulia Negura, who faces a four-year ban after testing positive for the anabolic steroid stanozolol.

Negura, the European cross country champion, has denied taking the drug, used by Ben Johnson before the Seoul Olympics where he tested positive after winning the men's 100 metres final in world record time.

Romanian athletics officials are struggling to cope with what local media call a "rash of doping cases", including nine supensions by the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF), over the past three years.
Only one of the cases has involved a man, former Balkan shot put champion Gheorghe Guset who was suspended in 1994.
The women include 17-year-old Mariana Florea, who won and lost her 400 metres gold medal at the European junior championships in San Sebastian, Spain, four years ago when she failed a doping test.
Appearance money, described by Balas as an "unofficial quota for attending international events", has been a major incentive to succeed.
Long jumper Marieta Ilcu saw her money jump from $1,000 to around $6,000 after she became world indoor in Toronto, Canada, in 1993.
Ilcu's career came to a dishonourable end in 1995, when she tested positive.
Last year the Romanian federation also slapped a life ban on marathon runner Elena Murgoci, 34, over the use of steroids.
